{{Short description|Smallest dimension where a graph can be represented as an intersection graph of boxes}}
{{Dark mode invert|[[File:Boxicity.svg|thumb|310px|Example of an intersection graph of axis-parallel rectangles with boxicity two]]}}

In the mathematical field of [[graph theory]], the '''boxicity''' of a [[Graph theory|graph]] is a [[graph invariant]] defined to be the minimum [[dimension]] of [[Euclidean space]] required to represent the graph as an [[intersection graph]] of axis-parallel [[Closed set|closed]] [[Box (shape)|boxes]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Roberts|1969|page=302|loc=Section 1}} uses closed cubes (of side-length <math>1</math>) for cubicity, and a bit further, claims "The development for [boxicity] will be entirely analogous [to that for cubicity], […].".<br>Footnote 1 on p. 302: "Boxes are not necessarily closed, though it is not hard to show that if a representation [of the graph] is attainable with [open] boxes in <math>\mathrm{E}^d</math>, it is attainable with closed boxes in <math>\mathrm{E}^d</math>.".</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Chandran|Mathew|2009|page=2|loc=Section 1, Definition 3}} use [[Cartesian product]]s of closed intervals <math>[a_i, b_i]</math>.</ref> That is, there must exist a one-to-one correspondence between the [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] of the graph and these boxes, such that two boxes intersect if and only if there is an edge connecting the corresponding vertices.

Boxicity was introduced by [[Fred S. Roberts]] in 1969.<ref>{{harvtxt|Roberts|1969|pages=301–310}}</ref>

==Examples==
The figure above shows a graph with six vertices, and a representation of this graph as an intersection graph of six axis-parallel rectangles (two-dimensional boxes) on the [[Euclidean plane]]. This graph cannot be represented as an intersection graph of boxes in any lower dimension, so its boxicity is two.

[[Image:Interval graph.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|Example of an [[interval graph]] with boxicity one]]
The second figure shows a graph with seven vertices, and a representation of this graph as an intersection graph of seven intervals (one-dimensional boxes) on the real [[number line]]. This graph cannot be represented as an intersection graph of boxes in {{math|0}}-space = {{math|{0}}}, so its boxicity is one.

==Relation to certain graph classes==
This article only considers [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|simple, finite, undirected graphs]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Chandran|Mathew|2009|page=2|loc=Section 1}}</ref>

{{harvtxt|Roberts|1969}} showed that the graph with {{math|2''n''}} vertices formed by removing a [[perfect matching]] from a [[complete graph]] on {{math|2''n''}} vertices has boxicity exactly {{mvar|n}}: each pair of disconnected vertices must be represented by boxes that are separated in a different dimension than each other pair. A box representation of this graph with dimension exactly {{mvar|n}} can be found by thickening each of the {{math|2''n''}} facets — these are {{math|(''n''−1)}}-cubes — of an {{mvar|n}}-dimensional [[hypercube]] into an {{mvar|n}}-box. Because of these results, this graph has been called the ''Roberts graph'',<ref>E.g., see {{harvtxt|Chandran|Francis|Sivadasan|2010}} and {{harvtxt|Chandran|Sivadasan|2007}}.</ref> although it is better known as the '''cocktail party graph''' and it can also be understood as the [[Turán graph]] {{math|''T''(2''n'',''n'')}}.

The boxicity of a complete graph is defined to be zero.<ref>{{harvtxt|Chandran|Mathew|2009|page=2|loc=Section 1, Definition 3}}</ref><br>Moreover, {{math|box(''G'') {{=}} 0}} iff {{mvar|G}} is complete.<ref>{{harvtxt|Roberts|1969|page=308|loc=Section 5}}</ref>

A graph has boxicity at most one if and only if it is an [[interval graph]]; the boxicity of an arbitrary graph {{mvar|G}} is also the minimum number of interval graphs on the same set of vertices such that the intersection of the edge sets of the interval graphs is {{mvar|G}}. Every [[outerplanar graph]] has boxicity at most two,<ref>{{harvtxt|Scheinerman|1984}}</ref> and every [[planar graph]] has boxicity at most three.<ref>{{harvtxt|Thomassen|1986}}</ref>

If a [[bipartite graph]] has boxicity two, then it can be represented as an intersection graph of axis-parallel line segments in the plane (such a graph has ''grid dimension'' one).<ref>{{harvtxt|Bellantoni|Ben-Arroyo Hartman|Przytycka|Whitesides|1993}}</ref>

{{harvtxt|Adiga|Bhowmick|Chandran|2011}} proved that the boxicity of a bipartite graph {{mvar|G}} is within a factor {{math|2}} of the [[order dimension]] of the height-two [[partially ordered set]] associated to {{mvar|G}} as follows: the set of minimal elements corresponds to one partite set of {{mvar|G}}, the set of maximal elements corresponds to the second partite set of {{mvar|G}}, and two elements are comparable if the corresponding vertices are adjacent in {{mvar|G}}. Equivalently, the [[order dimension]] of a height-two [[partially ordered set]] {{mvar|P}} is within a factor {{math|2}} of the boxicity of the [[comparability graph]] of {{mvar|P}} (which is bipartite, since {{mvar|P}} has height two).

==Algorithmic results==
Many graph problems can be solved or approximated more efficiently for graphs with bounded boxicity than they can for other graphs; for instance, the [[maximum clique problem]] can be solved in polynomial time for graphs with bounded boxicity.<ref>{{harvtxt|Chandran|Francis|Sivadasan|2010}} observe that this follows from the fact that these graphs have a polynomial number of [[maximal clique]]s, i.e., the class of graphs with bounded boxicity is said to have [[Graphs with few cliques|few cliques.]] An explicit box representation is not needed to list all maximal cliques efficiently.</ref> For some other graph problems, an efficient solution or approximation can be found if a low-dimensional box representation is known.<ref>See, e.g., {{harvtxt|Agarwal|van Kreveld|Suri|1998}} and {{harvtxt|Berman|DasGupta|Muthukrishnan|Ramaswami|2001}} for approximations to the [[maximum independent set]] for intersection graphs of rectangles, and {{harvtxt|Chlebík|Chlebíková|2005}} for results on hardness of approximation of these problems in higher dimensions.</ref> However, finding such a representation may be difficult: it is [[NP-complete]] to test whether the boxicity of a given graph is at most some given value {{mvar|K}}, even for {{math|''K'' {{=}} 2}}.<ref>{{harvtxt|Cozzens|1981}} shows that computing the boxicity is NP-complete; {{harvtxt|Yannakakis|1982}} shows that even checking whether the boxicity is at most {{math|3}} is NP-hard; finally, {{harvtxt|Kratochvil|1994}} shows that recognizing boxicity {{math|2}} is NP-hard.</ref> {{harvtxt|Chandran|Francis|Sivadasan|2010}} describe algorithms for finding representations of arbitrary graphs as intersection graphs of boxes, with a dimension that is within a [[logarithm]]ic factor of the [[Degree (graph theory)|maximum degree]] of the graph; this result provides an upper bound on the graph's boxicity.

Despite being hard for its natural parameter, boxicity is [[Parameterized complexity|fixed-parameter tractable]] when parameterized by the [[vertex cover]] number of the input graph.<ref>{{harvtxt|Adiga|Chitnis|Saurabh|2010}}</ref>

==Bounds==
For any graph <math>G</math>, <math>~ \operatorname{box}(G) \le \operatorname{tw}(G) + 2</math>, where <math>\operatorname{tw}(G)</math> denotes the [[treewidth]] of <math>G</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Chandran|Sivadasan|2007|loc=Theorem 14}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Chandran|Mathew|2009|page=3|loc=Section 2.1}}</ref>

If a graph <math>G</math> has <math>m</math> edges, then <math>\operatorname{box}(G) = O \left( \sqrt{m \log m} \right)</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Chandran|Francis|Sivadasan|2010}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Esperet|2016}}</ref>

If a graph <math>G</math> is <math>k</math>-[[Degeneracy (graph theory)|degenerate]] (with <math>k \ge 2</math>) and has <math>n</math> vertices, then <math>\operatorname{box}(G) \le (k+2) \lceil 2 \mathrm{e} \log n \rceil</math>,<ref>{{harvtxt|Adiga|Chandran|Mathew|2014}}</ref> where <math>\lceil \cdot \rceil</math> denotes the [[ceiling function]].

If a graph <math>G</math> has no complete graph on <math>t</math> vertices as a [[Graph minor|minor]], then <math>\operatorname{box}(G) = O(t^2 \log t)</math>,<ref>{{harvtxt|Esperet|Wiechert|2018}}</ref> while there are graphs with no complete graph on <math>t</math> vertices as a minor, and with <math>\operatorname{box}(G) = \Omega \left( t \cdot \sqrt{\log t} \right)</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Esperet|2016}}</ref> In particular, any graph <math>G</math> has <math>\operatorname{box}(G) = O \left( \mu(G)^2 \log \mu(G) \right)</math>, where <math>\mu(G)</math> denotes the [[Colin de Verdière graph invariant|Colin de Verdière invariant]] of <math>G</math>.

==Related graph invariants==
* [[Cubicity]] is defined in the same way as boxicity but with axis-parallel unit [[hypercube]]s instead of axis-parallel hyperrectangles.<!--The cubicity cub(G) of a graph G is the minimum dimension k such that G is representable as the intersection graph of axis-parallel unit cubes in k-dimensional space.--> Boxicity is a generalization of cubicity.
* [[Sphericity (graph theory)|Sphericity]] is defined in the same way as boxicity but with [[Congruence (geometry)|congruent]] [[sphere]]s.<!--The sphericity sph(G) of a graph G is the smallest n such that the vertices in G can be mapped into congruent spheres in n-space in such a way that two vertices are adjacent in G if and only if their assigned spheres intersect.-->
